title: Not quite eye to A.I.: student and teacher perspectives on the use of generative artificial intelligence in the writing process
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper examines how undergraduate students and teachers perceive the appropriate use of generative AI (GenAI), specifically ChatGPT, across stages of the writing process. The authors focus on a practical and policy-oriented question: when is it acceptable for a person to use GenAI to brainstorm, outline, write, revise, provide feedback, or evaluate writing, and how do students and teachers differ in those judgments?

The study used a cross-sectional questionnaire design with 226 participants: 158 students and 68 teachers. Students were recruited from a public research university in the United States, while teachers were recruited through purposive and snowball sampling from multiple institutions worldwide; most teachers were teaching adult/university-level English as a new language or modern languages. Participants rated example ChatGPT prompts and outputs that represented different levels of use or misuse, including use as a model, use with disclosure, and use without disclosure. The questionnaire also included survey items about attitudes toward AI, familiarity with AI, and whether participants’ institutions had AI policies or training.

Results showed broad agreement that GenAI is more acceptable when used as support for brainstorming, outlining, or modeling ideas, and less acceptable when it is used to fully complete writing assignments or when AI-generated text is submitted without disclosure. Teachers and students were generally aligned, but students tended to be somewhat more permissive about undisclosed use, while teachers were somewhat more accepting of GenAI as a model for feedback and evaluation. The authors conclude that GenAI needs clear policies, transparency requirements, and teacher professional development, since both groups reported high concern but low institutional preparedness, little AI training, and limited policy guidance.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed cross-sectional questionnaire study using descriptive statistics, Mann–Whitney U tests, and factor analysis, but it is not an experimental or causal design. Evidence quality is therefore correlational and perceptual rather than intervention-based.
impact_tier_rationale: The study does not report achievement or behavioral effect sizes from an implemented intervention, only acceptability and preparedness perceptions. Any educational impact is therefore indirect and unclear, though the policy implications are relevant.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a generative AI chatbot to support or perform writing-process tasks such as brainstorming, outlining, drafting, revising, giving feedback, and evaluating student writing.

finding.finding_summary: This study did not measure writing performance gains; instead, it assessed educators’ and students’ perceptions of acceptable GenAI use in the writing process (n=226; students n=158, teachers n=68). Both groups viewed GenAI as more acceptable for brainstorming/outlining and less acceptable for drafting or revising full essays, especially without disclosure. Significant between-group differences appeared on several items, e.g. teachers were more negative about GenAI-written essays with disclosure and without disclosure, while students were more accepting of some uses.
finding.measure: Likert-scale acceptability ratings for GenAI use across brainstorming, outlining, writing, revising, feedback, and evaluation tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper found a strong perceived lack of preparedness at the institutional level for GenAI in writing education. About 94.1% of teachers reported their institution had no AI policy and 95.6% reported no AI training; around 89.7% had not educated students about appropriate AI use. The authors conclude that explicit policies, training, and disclosure guidelines are urgently needed.
finding.measure: Yes/no survey items on institutional AI policy, AI training, and teacher education of students about AI use
